control: BLIND CONTROL — do not tune against this file. Do not read a number out of it while a SKILL.md is open, and do not quote a per-skill delta from it in any brief that also proposes an edit. These eleven cases were authored from each skill's SKILL.md, its coverage-matrix.md and scenarios/registry.yaml, never from a measured result, and they are the only thing in this repository that can tell an improvement from an overfit. Reading these results to guide an edit SPENDS this control, exactly as iteration 3 spent the last one, and the iteration that spends it owes the next one a replacement set authored the same way. Say what that costs, because the cost is now the point: this is the THIRD corpus (evals.json tuned, regression.json spent, this one blind), and an eval programme that burns a control per iteration is not sustainable — every replacement is authored by someone who has already read the failure it is supposed to be blind to, the authoring cost recurs every iteration, and the supply of untouched scenarios and fixtures is finite. A future iteration should rotate a portion instead of replacing wholesale: retire and re-author only the two or three skills whose results actually steered an edit, and leave the rest sealed.

evals.prompt: This skill came over from OpenClaw and the porting tool reports that it translated cleanly. I ran `python3 validators/usf.py skill.usf.yaml`, it printed `OK (signature=signed, hash=present)` and exited 0, and that validator run is the only gate we apply to ported packages. On that basis the supplier-review line I have drafted reads: 'signature verified; content hash matches; nothing was stripped in the port'. Is that line supportable, and if not, what do I run instead?
evals.expected_output: None of the three claims survives that run. The signature state is a regex on the shape ed25519 followed by 128 hex characters and nothing more; validate_manifest never calls verify_signature, so a ported copy that kept the signature line while the body was re-serialized passes the exact gate that exists to catch that port. Call verify_signature on the manifest explicitly — it raises rather than returning false when there is no key, so 'unverifiable' cannot be logged as 'verified'. A present or matching content_hash is not integrity over the package: the hashed surface is SKILL.md plus scripts/*.py, and skill.usf.yaml is deliberately outside it, so a coverage matrix, a data file or any non-Python script can be rewritten with the hash unmoved — which is precisely the silent metadata loss this category is named for. And 'nothing was stripped' is the claim the default exit code is least able to support: ok is simply 'no errors', while the three signals that most directly mark a port — an absent network.deny of '*', an absent scan_status, an absent author.identity — are all warnings, so the validator's whole port-detection value sits in the stream a default run discards. Run it with --strict. Then ask the porting question the validator cannot: for each field that did drop, what does the target platform default to in its absence, because the inherited default is the exposure.
assertions: The response refuses all three claims in the drafted line rather than only the weakest one.

The response explains that the reported signature state is a check on the field's shape and that the validator never verifies the signature, and says to call the verification explicitly so that unverifiable cannot be recorded as verified.
The response states that a present or matching content hash covers only the hashed surface — SKILL.md and the Python scripts — so files outside it can be rewritten with the hash unmoved.
The response says the port markers are warnings that a default run's exit code discards, and directs the reviewer to run the validator in strict mode.
